title: Light from a supernova in our galaxy reached Earth in the 1600s, but dust hid it

cover.alt: Cassiopeia A in X-rays: a roughly round cloud of glowing blue filaments with a thin bright rim, scattered with stars.
cover.credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/SAO; optical: NASA/STScI; processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/J. Major, A. Jubett, K. Arcand · Public domain

body: Cassiopeia A is the wreck of a massive star about 11,000 light-years away. Tracing its debris back suggests the explosion’s light reached Earth some time in the 1600s (estimates centre on the 1660s), yet no one left a clear record of a new star. The likely reason is **dust** between us and it, which soaked up most of its visible light; John Flamsteed may have logged it in 1680 as a faint star, at a spot where no star is seen today. Today the debris is about 10 light-years across and still racing outwards at 4,000 to 6,000 km/s.

slides.alt: Chandra X-ray images of Cassiopeia A, a ball of blue glowing filaments, cycle from 2000 to 2019 as labelled in the corner; the filaments flicker and shift and the faint outer rim edges outwards.
slides.caption: Chandra X-ray images of Cassiopeia A from 2000 to 2019, shown in a repeating loop: the debris shifts and the outer blast wave keeps pushing outwards.
slides.credit: NASA/CXC/SAO; NASA/STScI; J. Major, A. Jubett, K. Arcand · Public domain · excerpt

slides.prompt: Cassiopeia A was first reported in 1948, long before anyone could see it well. What kind of telescope found it?
slides.detail: Martin Ryle and Francis Graham-Smith reported it as a radio source. It is the brightest radio source beyond the Solar System at frequencies below 1 GHz.

slides.heading: How fast Cassiopeia A’s debris is flying
slides.note: Speeds across the sky; the fastest knots range from 5,500 to 14,500 km/s

slides.question: Why did hardly anyone see Cassiopeia A explode?
options: Dust absorbed most of its light
It was hidden behind the Moon
slides.explanation: Interstellar dust between Earth and the star probably absorbed most of its visible light, so it never became the dazzling new star it might have been.
